title: Speak sweetly
hook: speak insipid words and body and mind grow insipid (Asa di Var, ang 473)

segments.voice: Yesterday, laaitbaaree: clean eyes, clean ears, no feeding on gossip. Today the var comes back to the tongue, by way of the kitchen.

Taste a spoonful of dal before the salt goes in. It isn't bad, exactly. It isn't poisoned or burned. It's just flat. Lifeless. You take one bite and push the bowl away. Punjabi has a word for that taste: fikka. Tea without sugar is fikka. A party where nobody talks is fikka. And Guru Nanak used the same kitchen word, in a salok of the Asa di Var, for a kind of speech. Not lying, which we met two days ago. Something more ordinary, and maybe more common.
screen: `DAL BEFORE THE SALT.` → `FIKKA: FLAT, TASTELESS.` → `A KITCHEN WORD FOR SPEECH.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 473. In paraphrase: speaking fikka words, the body and mind become fikka. The fikka person is called fikka; the fikka person gets a fikka name. The fikka are cast out of the Court of the Lord, and have their faces spat upon. The fikka are called fools, and are punished with shoes. The word repeats until you can taste it. Fikka here means insipid, but it leans toward harsh, rude, sour: words with no sweetness and no care in them. A curt reply. A sarcastic dig. A cold one-word answer to someone who needed more. Here's the turn. The salok doesn't only say fikka words hurt the listener. It says they make the speaker fikka, body and mind. Speak flat and sour long enough, and you become flat and sour. Your reputation follows: people start to call you that. Anyone who's watched a person harden over the years has seen it happen. Words aren't just output. They're practice. Every sentence trains the one who says it. This connects back to mitthat neevee from day five hundred fifty-one: sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue. That was about who you are. Today is about how you get there. Sweet speech isn't flattery or fake niceness. It means words with some care cooked into them. Salt in the dal. Sugar in the tea. Something that makes the other person want to stay at the table.
screen: `FIKKA: FLAT, HARSH, SOUR.` · `FIKKA WORDS MAKE A FIKKA PERSON.` · `EVERY SENTENCE IS PRACTICE.` · `CARE COOKED INTO WORDS.` · then, large: `SWEET WORDS, SWEET LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of the last flat or sharp thing you said to someone, and without scolding yourself, just hear it again. Now imagine it with care cooked in: the same truth, a warmer sentence. If you pray, say Waheguru first.
Speak sweetly. Guru Nanak's warning about fikka words, flat and harsh like dal without salt: they make the body and mind of the speaker fikka too.
Your line: sweet words, sweet life. Every sentence trains the one who says it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok on fikka speech in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and sweet, humble speech is counted among the marks of a Sikh's character.

trapdoor: what it means: flat, harsh words make the speaker flat and harsh; sweet words, with care in them, shape a sweet life.
what a scholar hears: the salok repeats fikka in nearly every phrase, so the sound itself turns sour; it pairs with mitthat neevee earlier in the var.

He says sweet speech means flattery: tell people what they want to hear to keep peace.
